item.research_question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?
item.material_system: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V)
item.processing_route: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.
item.test_conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s).
key_findings: Advanced LPBF samples achieved 95% density compared to 38% in primary trials and similar macrostructure to AMF counterparts.
Both LPBF and AMF alloys formed a single solid phase solution with BCC crystal structure and lattice parameter of 3.2 Å.
LPBF samples exhibited finer grain size (average 10 µm) compared to AMF samples (average 25 µm).
Ultimate compressive strength of LPBF sample was 1391 ± 166 MPa, higher than the AMF sample at 1107 ± 43 MPa.
LPBF sample density was 10.83 g/cm³, approximately 1.6% lower than the AMF sample at 11.01 g/cm³.
Both alloys showed excellent corrosion resistance with active-passive transition; LPBF had higher break potential (0.020 mA passivation current) but reduced stability due to roughness.
Local EDS analysis revealed tungsten enrichment (37.6 at.%) in specific grains and vanadium depletion in LPBF, while AMF showed significant V accumulation at grain boundaries (up to 66.9 at.%).
TEM analysis identified sub-grains of ~500 nm and spherical precipitates (60–80 nm) rich in V (33.2 at.%) and depleted in W (7.9 at.%) at intergranular boundaries in LPBF samples.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the elemental segregation (W enrichment in grains, V at boundaries) to the significant difference in melting temperatures between elements (W: 3422 °C vs. V: 1910 °C), causing V to solidify last at grain boundaries. The finer grain size and higher strength in LPBF are attributed to rapid solidification characteristics inherent to the process, while defects like porosity and unmelted particles contribute to brittleness.
item.limitations: The study notes that the LPBF process resulted in inherent printing defects such as porosity and unmelted powder particles, which induce brittleness and reduce passivation stability. Additionally, the mixed elemental powder had irregular particle shapes and size deviations (e.g., Ta standard deviation of 20%), leading to non-homogeneous compositions and uneven distribution of elements.
item.future_work: The authors state that additional experimental work is required to further optimize printing parameters to obtain improved properties and microstructure characteristics, mainly in terms of printing defects. They also propose including post-heat treatments to upgrade the homogeneity of the LPBF alloy and its synthesis characteristics.
quotes: The results disclosed similarities in microstructure, physical properties and electrochemical behavior between HEA WTaMoNbV manufactured by the proposed LPBF process and its counterpart alloy produced by an AMF process.
The ultimate compressive strength of the LPBF sample was slightly higher than the counterpart AMF sample, as shown in Table 10.
This can be attributed mainly to the relatively high melting temperature and high density of W compared to other alloying elements.
